title: Eight parts of a path
hookLine: the fourth truth: right view, intention, speech, action, livelihood, effort, mindfulness, concentration
last: A FLAME THAT HAS GONE OUT.

lines: THE FOURTH TRUTH IS A PATH.
cards: Three truths in, a practical question shows up. Suffering has a plain name. The thirst behind it has been found.
And it can end, like a lamp going out. So what happens on Wednesday morning, with the dishes, the commute and the email that needs answering? The Buddha's first teaching doesn't leave that hanging.
Its fourth truth isn't another idea. It's a path of eight parts, and most of them look a lot like an ordinary day.

teach.h: A MIDDLE WAY BETWEEN TWO ROADS.
teach.b: First, a middle way. In the Samyutta Nikaya, before he names any of the four truths, the Buddha names two roads to avoid: chasing sense pleasures, and tormenting yourself. Both, he says, are unprofitable.
Between them runs a middle way, and that middle way is this path.
Second, the eight parts. Right view. Right intention.
Right speech. Right action. Right livelihood.
Right effort. Right mindfulness. Right concentration.
Notice how few of them happen on a cushion. Speech is what comes out at the checkout. Action is what the hands do.
Livelihood is how the rent gets paid. Third, a nun sorts them.
In the Majjhima Nikaya, a layman puts questions to the nun Dhammadinna, and one of her answers groups the eight into three. Speech, action and livelihood belong to virtue.
Effort, mindfulness and concentration belong to concentration. View and intention belong to wisdom. So the path has a shape: how you live with others, how you train the mind, and how you see.
Fourth, one step at a time. This week circled the first three truths: the second arrow and the thirst, hatred that ends only by love, the mind that leads, Patacara's grief and her lamp.
What hurts, where it comes from, and that it can end. The fourth truth is the one you walk.
And a path of eight parts is still walked one step at a time, on one ordinary day, starting with whichever step the day hands you.

how: Buddhists study the noble eightfold path as the fourth noble truth; in daily life practitioners often work with one factor at a time, such as right speech or right livelihood, alongside meditation for effort, mindfulness and concentration.

o: the path between chasing pleasure and tormenting yourself
a habit of always splitting the difference in arguments
a calm halfway point found by doing nothing at all

games.q: inside the fourth truth — tap the pairs.

s: the eightfold path is only about meditation
speech, action and livelihood are three of the eight parts.
the Buddha calls the path a middle way between two roads
between chasing sense pleasures and tormenting yourself.
Dhammadinna puts speech, action and livelihood under wisdom
she puts them under virtue; view and intention go under wisdom.

games.q: you're one of the Buddha's first listeners. he names two roads to avoid: chasing sense pleasure, and tormenting yourself. what does he offer?
o: a little of each, in balance
the harder road, since pleasure is the trap
a middle way: a path with eight parts
games.why: he calls both roads unprofitable and names a middle way between them: the noble eightfold path, the fourth truth.

practice: Walk through the eight slowly, one per breath: view, intention, speech, action, livelihood, effort, mindfulness, concentration.

On the second time through, notice which one catches, maybe speech because of a conversation coming later, and let that one stay while the others rest. Then see where today will meet it: the room, the person, the hour.

wordCard.voice: Middle way, the Buddha's fourth noble truth: a path of eight parts, between chasing pleasure and tormenting yourself, walked one step at a time. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali, written here in Devanagari: the path with eight parts, from the Buddha's first teaching.

carryVoice: Your line: one step of eight. Seven days, four truths, one path. That's a week.
